# Acute otitis media

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Head and neck surgery > Acute otitis media*

[Original Article Link](/library/Mj0MaT)

---

## Summary

Acute <u>otitis media</u> (AOM) is a painful infection of the <u>middle ear</u> that most commonly results from a bacterial <u>superinfection</u> with <u>Streptococcus pneumoniae</u>, <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>, or <u>Moraxella catarrhalis</u> following a viral <u>upper respiratory tract infection</u> (<u>URTI</u>). AOM is a common infection in children under the age of 2 years and is characterized by an acute onset of symptoms (e.g., <u>otalgia</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>anorexia</u>) with signs of <u>middle ear</u> inflammation (e.g., bulging <u>tympanic membrane</u>, <u>erythema</u>). Mild unilateral infections can be managed without <u>antibiotics</u>, as they are often <u>self-limited</u>. Infections in children under 6 months, bilateral AOM, or severe symptoms are usually treated with oral <u>antibiotics</u>. Most children will experience at least one episode before the age of five; in children with <u>recurrent AOM</u> that causes frequent symptoms, <u>myringotomy</u> and insertion of <u>tympanostomy</u> tubes may be considered. The most common complication is acute <u>mastoiditis</u>, but <u>facial palsy</u>, <u>labyrinthitis</u>, and in rare cases, even intracranial <u>abscesses</u> may also occur.




See also “<u>Otitis media with effusion</u>” and “<u>Chronic suppurative otitis media</u>.”

---

## Epidemiology

* Highest <u>incidence</u> between 6–24 months of age [[1]](/library/rSVfa80)[[2]](/library/lmbvf8)

* Approx. 50–80% of children ≤ 3 years old experience AOM at least once.  [[2]](/library/lmbvf8)[[3]](/library/xucEtV0)

* Slightly higher <u>incidence</u> in boys [[3]](/library/xucEtV0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

* The <u>eustachian tube</u> connects the <u>middle ear</u> with the <u>nasopharynx</u> and is lined with <u>cilia</u>, which drain the <u>middle ear</u> secretions into the <u>nasopharynx</u>.

* Obstruction/blockage of the <u>eustachian tube</u> (ET) → lack of ventilation and drainage of the <u>middle ear</u> →

* Resorption of the air in the <u>middle ear</u> → negative <u>middle ear</u> pressure → <u>retraction</u> of the <u>tympanic membrane</u> → <u>otalgia</u> and <u>conductive hearing loss</u>

* Accumulation of <u>middle ear</u> secretions → bacterial <u>superinfection</u> → <u>pus</u> in the <u>middle ear</u> → bulging <u>tympanic membrane</u> → severe <u>otalgia</u>, <u>fever</u>

* Predisposing factors for ET obstruction

* Inflammation of the ET <u>mucosa</u>

* Viral URT infection (most common cause)

* <u>Allergic rhinitis</u>

* Mechanical obstruction of the ET

* <u>Enlarged adenoids</u>

* <u>Nasal polyps</u>

* <u>Cleft palate</u>

* <u>Infants</u>: shorter, less rigid, and more horizontal ET → <u>nasopharyngeal</u> secretions easily reflux into the ET → more <u>prone</u> to developing AOM





References:[[4]](/library/6H0jrh)[[5]](/library/JH0srh)

---

## Etiology

### Common pathogens [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)




* General considerations

* <u>Coinfection</u> with both bacterial and viral pathogens is common (∼ 66% of cases).

* Purely bacterial AOM is less common (27% of cases).

* Purely viral AOM is rare (< 8%).  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[7]](/library/7SV4a80)

* Bacterial pathogens [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)

* <u>S. pneumoniae</u>  [[2]](/library/lmbvf8)

* <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>  [[8]](/library/Nmb-f8)

* <u>Moraxella catarrhalis</u>

* <u>Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci</u>: rare (< 5% of cases) [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[9]](/library/Bedza60)

* Viral pathogens [[10]](/library/35YSPp)

* <u>Respiratory syncytial virus</u>

* <u>Parainfluenza virus</u>

* <u>Influenza virus</u>

* <u>Rhinovirus</u>

* <u>Adenovirus</u>





### Risk factors for AOM [[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[11]](/library/qraCRN)




* Passive <u>cigarette smoke</u>

* Children who attend daycare centers

* Formula feeding/bottle feeding  [[12]](/library/xNbEW8)

* Pacifier use

* Children who have more than one sibling or live in a crowded space

* Male sex

* Family or personal history of AOM

* Anatomical abnormalities

* Feeding in a <u>supine position</u>  [[13]](/library/BNbzW8)

---

## Clinical features

Older children and adults will most frequently report <u>ear</u> <u>pain</u>; in <u>infants</u> and nonverbal children symptoms can be nonspecific, and may be easily confused with other conditions.




### General symptoms [[10]](/library/35YSPp)




* <u>Otalgia</u>/earache, commonly described as throbbing <u>pain</u>

* <u>Hearing loss</u> in the affected <u>ear</u>

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Otorrhea</u> in the case of a <u>ruptured tympanic membrane</u> (TM)





#### Typical presentation in <u>infants</u> [[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[11]](/library/qraCRN)




* Irritability

* Incessant crying

* Refusal to feed (<u>anorexia</u>)

* Repeatedly touching the affected <u>ear</u>

* <u>Fever</u> and <u>febrile seizures</u>

* <u>Vomiting</u>





### Examination findings [[10]](/library/35YSPp)




#### <u>Otoscopy</u>




* Bulging <u>tympanic membrane</u> (TM) with loss of landmarks  [[14]](/library/dnboH8)

* Opacification and loss of light reflex

* <u>Retracted</u> and hypomobile TM

* <u>Purulent</u>/serosanguinous discharge in the <u>external auditory canal</u> or visible perforation

* Distinct <u>erythema</u> of the TM    [[10]](/library/35YSPp)

* Additional findings that may be present:

* Yellow spot on the TM  [[15]](/library/Dnb1v8)

* Cartwheel TM  [[15]](/library/Dnb1v8)

* <u>Blisters</u> or <u>bullae</u> on the <u>tympanic membrane</u>   [[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[16]](/library/3mbS28)

#### <u>Tuning fork test</u>



* The <u>Weber test</u> and <u>Rinne test</u> can be performed to verify <u>conductive hearing loss</u> secondary to an effusion. [[17]](/library/_5b558)

* <u>Weber test</u>: Sound localizes to the affected <u>ear</u>.

* <u>Rinne test</u>: Air conduction is impaired in the affected <u>ear</u>, while bone conduction remains intact.

---

## Diagnosis

AOM is primarily a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on characteristic symptoms and otoscopic findings. Other causes of <u>otalgia</u> and <u>hearing loss</u> should be excluded (see “Differential diagnoses”). <u>Pneumatic otoscopy</u> or <u>tympanometry</u> should be used to confirm the presence of an effusion. [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)




### Diagnostic criteria for AOM in children  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[10]](/library/35YSPp)




The diagnosis of AOM can be made if any of the following features are present:  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)




* Moderate to severe bulging of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>

* New onset of <u>otorrhea</u> not due to <u>otitis externa</u>

* New onset of <u>otalgia</u> AND mild bulging of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>

* Distinct <u>erythema</u> AND mild bulging of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>





### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




Not routinely indicated; consider in severe infection or diagnostic uncertainty.




* <u>CBC</u>: <u>Leukocytosis</u> may be present.

* <u>Gram stain</u> and culture of <u>middle ear</u> fluid  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)

* Indication: patients who do not respond to initial therapy, acutely ill patients, and patients with <u>immune deficiencies</u> [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[18]](/library/FObg8F)

* Typically acquired through tympanocentesis: the extraction of <u>middle ear</u> fluid through a small-gauge needle.

* Fluid should also be cultured if there is <u>otorrhea</u> from <u>tympanostomy</u> tubes or a <u>perforated TM</u>.  [[18]](/library/FObg8F)

* <u>Blood cultures</u>: indicated only in severe infection





### Imaging [[19]](/library/Qmbu28)




* Rarely required unless there is clinical uncertainty and/or concerns of complications

* Suspected intracranial complications: <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> and <u>temporal bone</u>

* Suspected extracranial complications, e.g., <u>mastoiditis</u>: high-resolution CT <u>temporal bone</u>





### Evaluation for effusion




* Pneumatic otoscopy [[20]](/library/U5bbj8) 

* Description

* A pneumatic bulb is attached to the otoscope to allow assessment of <u>tympanic membrane</u> mobility.

* A seal is formed in <u>the ear</u> canal by the tip of the speculum, and air is forced in by pressing the bulb.

* Indications: clinical uncertainty for AOM and to confirm the presence of <u>middle ear</u> effusion

* Characteristic finding: hypomobility of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>  [[21]](/library/bnbH78)

* <u>Tympanometry</u> [[22]](/library/VnbGH8) 

* Description: a probe is inserted into <u>the ear</u> to generate sound waves and measure pressure in <u>the ear</u> canal

* Indications: confirmation of <u>middle ear</u> effusion  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[22]](/library/VnbGH8)

* Characteristic findings

* High <u>peak pressure</u> reflecting the bulging of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>

* Flattened curve indicating effusion

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[10]](/library/35YSPp)




* Screen patients for acute complications such as <u>mastoiditis</u> and <u>labyrinthitis</u> and treat if present.

* Provide <u>analgesia</u> as needed.

* Consider <u>antibiotic therapy</u> based on the patient's age and clinical features.

* Children < 2 years of age: Generally give <u>antibiotics</u>.

* Children ≥ 2 years of age

* Severe symptoms and/or <u>otorrhea</u>: Give <u>antibiotics</u>.

* Mild symptoms and no <u>otorrhea</u>: <u>conservative management</u>  [[23]](/library/AucRFV0)[[24]](/library/yucdFV0)

* Adults: <u>Antibiotics</u> are typically given.  [[3]](/library/xucEtV0)[[25]](/library/BucztV0)

* Reassess all patients <u>managed conservatively</u> after 48–72 hours; if there is no improvement, give <u>antibiotics</u>.

* Consult ENT for adults with <u>recurrent AOM</u> or persistent <u>otitis media with effusion</u>. [[3]](/library/xucEtV0)





### <u>Conservative management</u>




Uncomplicated AOM is <u>self-limiting</u> in most children (∼ 80%). [[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[11]](/library/qraCRN)




* Outpatient observation and surveillance of symptoms for 48–72 hours

* <u>Oral analgesia</u>  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)

* <u>Acetaminophen</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE

* No sufficient evidence to support the routine use of <u>opioids</u>, decongestants, <u>antihistamines</u>, <u>steroids</u> [[11]](/library/qraCRN)





> [!TIP]
> Many patients with AOM can be <u>treated conservatively</u>. [[10]](/library/35YSPp)




### <u>Antibiotic</u> treatment




Systemic <u>antibiotic therapy</u> in AOM is recommended to relieve symptoms and reduce the risk of complications in young <u>infants</u> and patients with severe infections. [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)




* Topical <u>antibiotics</u> are typically reserved for patients with AOM and <u>tympanostomy</u> tubes (see “Special situations”) or those with <u>chronic suppurative otitis media</u>. [[26]](/library/ZEcZ8V0)

* Treatment failure is common (due to drug resistance and viral <u>coinfection</u>); If initial treatment is unsuccessful, consider <u>tympanocentesis</u> to help guide further therapy.

* Typical duration of first-line therapy  [[3]](/library/xucEtV0)

* Children < 2 years OR any child with severe symptoms: 10 days

* Children ≥ 2 years AND no severe symptoms: 5–7 days





> [!TIP]
> Topical <u>antibiotics</u> are generally ineffective in treating AOM unless <u>tympanostomy</u> tubes are present.




#### Indications




* Children  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[10]](/library/35YSPp)

* Age ≤ 6 months

* Age < 2 years with bilateral AOM  [[3]](/library/xucEtV0)[[6]](/library/sH0t7h)[[11]](/library/qraCRN)

* Any age with:

* Symptoms that have not improved after 48–72 hours

* Severe AOM

* Signs of severe systemic illness

* <u>Otorrhea</u> not due to <u>otitis externa</u>

* <u>Cochlear implants</u>  [[27]](/library/RLblx8)

* Adults: <u>Antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>amoxicillin</u>) are typically given to prevent complications.  [[3]](/library/xucEtV0)[[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[11]](/library/qraCRN)[[25]](/library/BucztV0)





> [!WARNING]
> Children with <u>cochlear implants</u> who develop AOM should always be treated with <u>antibiotics</u>.




#### Regimens




> [!TIP]
> <u>Amoxicillin</u> is the first-line agent in <u>antibiotic</u>-naive patients. A <u>macrolide</u> can be given if the patient is severely allergic to <u>penicillin</u>.

### Surgical procedures for AOM




* Indications

* Not routinely indicated in acute AOM

* Consider for patients with treatment failure or recurrent infection.

* Procedures

* Myringotomy [[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[28]](/library/KMbUp8)

* Surgical <u>incision</u> into the <u>tympanic membrane</u> to drain fluid to relieve pressure/<u>pain</u>

* Consider as an adjunct to <u>antibiotic therapy</u> for severe <u>otalgia</u> and a bulging <u>tympanic membrane</u>  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)

* <u>Myringotomy</u> with tympanostomy tube insertion  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)

* Placement of small tubes into the <u>tympanic membrane</u> to prevent the accumulation of fluid

* Consider for <u>otitis media with effusion</u> and in children with recurrent AOM  [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)





![Myringotomy with tympanostomy tube insertion](media/amoksnrge7qe4x2r0q5etarv.jpg)

Myringotomy with tympanostomy tube insertion




### Special situations




* AOM with <u>perforated tympanic membrane</u>

* Usually (> 90%) heals spontaneously with systemic <u>antibiotic therapy</u> (See “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for AOM</u>.”)  [[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[29]](/library/p5bLO8)

* There is no added advantage of topical <u>antibiotics for AOM</u> with <u>TM perforation</u> unless <u>tympanostomy</u> tubes are present. [[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[30]](/library/Euc8GV0)[[31]](/library/vucAGV0)

* <u>The ear</u> should be kept clean and dry  until the TM has fully healed. [[32]](/library/webhaG)

* Patients with <u>tympanostomy</u> tubes [[10]](/library/35YSPp)

* Increased discharge indicates acute infection.

* Usually caused by the same spectrum of bacterial pathogens, but <u>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</u>, <u>Staphylococcus aureus</u>, and <u>Staphylococcus epidermidis</u> are also possible

* Can be treated with topical <u>antibiotics</u> for 7 days (e.g., <u>ofloxacin</u> DOSAGE, <u>ciprofloxacin</u>/<u>dexamethasone</u> DOSAGE [[10]](/library/35YSPp)

* If there are complications or systemic illness, oral <u>antibiotics</u> (normally <u>amoxicillin/clavulanic acid</u> DOSAGE) can be given. [[10]](/library/35YSPp)

---

## Complications

<u>Otitis media</u> can spread to affect other local structures (e.g., <u>mastoiditis</u>, <u>labyrinthitis</u>, <u>facial nerve palsy</u>, <u>perforated tympanic membrane</u>) or the intracranial cavity (e.g., <u>meningitis</u>, <u>cerebral venous thrombosis</u>, <u>otogenic abscess</u>).




### <u>Risk factors</u> for complications




Complications are rare and are usually only seen in the following cases:




* Highly <u>virulent</u> bacteria (e.g., Group A ß-<u>hemolytic</u> <u>streptococci</u>)

* <u>Immunocompromised</u> patients

* Inadequate dose/duration of <u>antibiotics</u>

* Bacterial drug resistance





### Bacterial labyrinthitis




* Etiology: Inflammation spreads to the <u>inner ear</u> (labyrinth) through the <u>round window</u>.

* Clinical features

* Severe <u>vertigo</u>, <u>nausea</u>, and <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Hearing loss</u>

* <u>Nystagmus</u> direction can be variable  [[33]](/library/_uc5FV0)[[34]](/library/zucrFV0)

* Diagnostics

* Change of lateralization in <u>Weber test</u>

* <u>Audiometry</u>: <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u>

* Treatment

* IV <u>antibiotics</u> + <u>tympanostomy</u> with insertion of <u>tympanostomy</u> tube + <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* <u>Mastoidectomy</u> (to treat the source of infection in AOM)





### <u>Peripheral facial palsy</u> [[35]](/library/fLbkC8)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: Rare complication in the <u>antibiotic</u> era

* Etiology: unclear

* Clinical features: <u>lower motor neuron</u> <u>paralysis</u> of <u>cranial nerve VII</u>

* Diagnostics:

* <u>High-resolution CT</u> of <u>temporal bones</u> to rule out concurrent <u>mastoiditis</u> [[36]](/library/ULbbC8)

* <u>Electroneurography</u>: patients with > 95% degeneration at 3– 14 days after <u>paralysis</u> develops require surgical decompression [[35]](/library/fLbkC8)

* Treatment:

* IV <u>cephalosporin</u> (e.g. <u>cefotaxime</u> DOSAGE or <u>ceftazidime</u> DOSAGE) [[35]](/library/fLbkC8)

* <u>Corticosteroids</u> DOSAGE  [[37]](/library/2LbTC8)

* Surgical decompression of the nerve





### Otogenic abscess




* Route of spread: direct spread of infection from the <u>middle ear</u> through the destroyed bone overlying the <u>dura</u> or through an <u>emissary vein</u>

* Types

* Epidural <u>abscess</u>

* Subdural <u>abscess</u>

* <u>Cerebral abscess</u>: The <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>temporal lobe</u> is the most common site (<u>ipsilateral</u> <u>cerebellar</u> <u>abscess</u> is second most common).

* Clinical features

* Persistent <u>headache</u> and <u>otorrhea</u>

* <u>Signs of raised ICP</u>

* <u>Signs of meningeal irritation</u>

* <u>Focal neurological deficits</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>MRI</u>/<u>contrast-enhanced CT</u>

* Treatment: IV <u>antibiotics</u> + drainage + <u>mastoidectomy</u>





### Other intracranial complications




* See “<u>Meningitis</u>.”

* See “<u>Cerebral venous thrombosis</u>.”





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prevention

* Recommend:

* <u>Exclusive breastfeeding</u> for at least 6 months

* <u>Smoking cessation</u> for caregivers

* Advise limiting pacifier use and avoiding <u>supine</u> bottle feeding.

* Encourage adherence to the <u>ACIP immunization schedule</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Day care attendance is associated with an increased risk of AOM. [[6]](/library/sH0t7h)

---
